sections.html:
Nevada's southernmost county is also its biggest by population: 2,265,461 people in 2020, roughly 70% of the state, living on 8,061 square miles of land. Las Vegas is the seat. Henderson, North Las Vegas, Boulder City and Mesquite round out five incorporated cities, and 21 unincorporated towns fill in much of the rest.

Sellers should know one quirk. Over a million people in unincorporated areas still receive mail addressed to Las Vegas. Your property might fall under a city or under an unincorporated town, and that decides which planning, code and utility offices you work with. The county bills the tax in both cases.

Responsibility is divided three ways at the county. The Assessor determines value. The Treasurer sends the bill and receives the payment. The Recorder files the deed and collects transfer tax. Rates for each tax district come from the state Department of Taxation.

  • Treasurer mailing address: 500 S Grand Central Pkwy, Box 551220, Las Vegas, NV 89155-1220
  • Treasurer phone: (702) 455-4323, Monday through Thursday, 7:30 am to 5:30 pm; closed Friday through Sunday
  • Assessor appeals line: (702) 455-4997

Bills for real property go out once a fiscal year. Nothing in your mailbox by August 1? The automated phone system can send a copy. Under NRS 361.480, a bill that never came is not a defense for paying late. New owners who bought partway through the year, and owners whose lender quit paying, should call and ask for a bill.

Payment of the whole bill is due on the third Monday in August. If the total exceeds $100 you can split it, though the county is clear that these are not quarterly payments. The split schedule runs August (third Monday), October, January and March (each first Monday). A 10-day window follows each date before any penalty attaches, and the penalty compounds as installments pile up:

Installments latePenalty on each late installment
One4%
Two9% on the first, 5% on the second
Three15%, 11% and 6%
Four22%, 18%, 13% and 7%

Homeowners with an escrow account should still verify that their servicer paid on time, since the county treats the owner as accountable. Email and text reminders can be set up through the Treasurer's page.

By the end of April, parcels with unpaid tax are published as delinquent, both in the local paper and online at the Treasurer's site. A balance that survives to close of business on the first Monday in June puts the property into a two-year redemption period held by the Treasurer.

The owner buys the property back by paying taxes, accruing taxes, penalties and costs, with 10% interest per year from the original due date. A property found abandoned can be handled on a one-year track under NRS 361.567. If nobody pays, the deed goes to the County Treasurer acting as trustee, and the parcel can be put up at auction.

The county typically holds an auction at least yearly, often in spring, capping registration at 280 bidders and asking a $5,000 deposit. A property becomes eligible once it has been deeded to the trustee after three consecutive delinquent fiscal years, or two if it was abandoned.

You can still sell a house that is on a delinquent list before redemption ends. The closing pays off what is owed. The county keeps current rules on its real property tax page.

sections.h2: How is my home valued, and how do I appeal?
sections.html:
The cost method drives the Assessor's number. Staff estimate what it would take to rebuild the structure today, take off depreciation at 1.5% for each year of effective age (stopping at 50 years), then add what the land would sell for. The whole calculation is redone each year.

Because the rate depends on your tax district, your neighbor across a district line may pay differently. A home that qualifies for the 3% or 8% abatement pays whichever is lower, the calculated tax or the capped amount.

  • Forms: the Assessor has appeal forms in December.
  • Deadline: January 15, shifting to the next business day if it hits a weekend or holiday.
  • Next steps: if the County Board of Equalization agrees with the Assessor, you can go to the State Board, then to District Court.

Before filing, gather photos, repair quotes and recent sale prices of similar houses nearby. A call to the appeals line often settles a simple error without a hearing.

The Recorder collects $2.55 per $500 of value, counting a partial $500 as a full unit. The base is the full purchase price or estimated fair market value. Nevada's base rate is $1.95 per $500 statewide, and Clark County tacks on $0.60.

NRS 375.090 exempts certain transfers. Every deed needs a Declaration of Value, which the Recorder hands out free. An online calculator gives a rough figure, but your title company produces the final amount on the settlement statement.

Tax debt gets settled at the table just as any lien would. The title company requests a payoff figure from the Treasurer, subtracts it from what you receive, and apportions the current installment between buyer and seller. If you are behind, check your parcel on the Treasurer's payment site first to see which installments are open.

Watch the calendar. A contract signed in September can run straight into the October installment, and each party owes a share of the year. If an escrow lender skipped a payment, correct that before closing day, because a surprise balance can stall the deal.

Collect your deed, your newest tax statement, a lender payoff letter if you have a mortgage, and any delinquency notice. Hand these to the title company early. A clean file shortens the wait between an accepted offer and the money in your account.

sections.h2: What Clark County sellers run into
sections.html:
Scale causes most of the trouble. A sale that works smoothly in one tax district can hit an unexpected snag in another, so confirm the details for your own parcel instead of assuming. Sellers who treat the Treasurer, Assessor and Recorder as three separate stops usually avoid the worst delays: one stop for the balance, one for any value dispute or abatement question, and one for the deed paperwork.

  • Rates differ by district, so you cannot copy a neighbor's bill.
  • An installment can fall due right after you sign.
  • Escrow lenders sometimes miss a payment.
  • Heirs may inherit a house with several unpaid installments.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is anywhere in the county and can close around a tax balance, taking the payoff from the sale. We name no price until we have seen the property. For a first step, look up your parcel on the Treasurer's payment site and write down what is open.

faqs.q: When are Clark County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Due in full on the third Monday in August. Bills over $100 can be paid across four dates instead, adding the first Mondays of October, January and March. Each date has a 10-day cushion.

faqs.q: What does a late payment cost in Clark County?
faqs.a: A single late installment adds 4%. Two late means 9% on the first and 5% on the second, and the percentages keep climbing at three and four.

faqs.q: What transfer tax applies in Clark County?
faqs.a: $2.55 for every $500 of value, built from the $1.95 state base plus a $0.60 county add-on.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my assessment in Clark County?
faqs.a: File with the County Board of Equalization by January 15. Forms appear in December, and the Assessor's appeals line is (702) 455-4997.

faqs.q: Can I sell if my Clark County taxes are delinquent?
faqs.a: Yes, so long as the sale closes before redemption ends. What you owe in tax, penalties and interest is taken from the sale proceeds.
